misconception_description: Student believes that conditional statements, i.e., Python statements that evaluate to either True or False, must always be wrapped in if/else statements to be returned as Boolean values.

solutions.generated_code:
program CekBilanganPrima
kamus
  n, i : integer
  prima, valid : boolean
algoritma
  input(n)
  if n >= 2 then
    valid <- true
  else
    valid <- false
  endif
  if valid == false then
    prima <- false
  else
    prima <- true
    for i <- 2 to n - 1 do
      if n mod i == 0 then
        prima <- false
      endif
    endfor
  endif
  output(prima)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student exhibits the misconception by unnecessarily wrapping boolean conditions in if/else statements instead of using the boolean expressions directly. At the beginning, instead of just checking the condition inline, they explicitly assign True/False to is_valid based on if/else. They also check `is_valid == False` with another if statement instead of directly using the boolean. At the end, instead of simply `return True`, they wrap it in `if num >= 2: return True else: return False` even though the code has already verified num >= 2 earlier. From the student's perspective, this is the proper way to handle boolean values - they must be explicitly checked with if/else to return True or False, rather than returning the boolean expression directly.
